opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it was my family. My parents were pretty open-minded about education, and they never framed the gaokao as the single path that would determine my whole life. So when the opportunity came up to go abroad and study, it didn't feel like I was betraying some expectation or giving up on something sacred. It just felt like another option, and honestly a more interesting one for me.

The other part is personality. I've always been a bit stubborn about doing things that make sense to me rather than doing them because everyone else is. In high school, I could see my classmates grinding through practice exams day and night, and I respected that, but I also knew that wasn't where my curiosity was. I was more excited about building things, tinkering with computers, reading about technology. The idea of spending two or three years optimizing for one exam just didn't resonate with me.

And I think when you're young, not knowing exactly what the risks are actually helps. I wasn't overthinking it. I didn't have this sense of, "What if it doesn't work out?" I just thought, okay, this path seems like it'll let me explore more, so let's try it. Looking back, that kind of naive confidence was probably a gift. It let me take a step that, if I'd been more anxious about it, I might not have taken.

r001.rationale: He says his curiosity lay elsewhere and that spending years preparing for the gaokao did not resonate with him.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think a lot of it came down to the fact that I never saw the gaokao as the only door. Growing up, my family was pretty relaxed about it. My parents never sat me down and said, "This one exam decides your life." They cared more about whether I was actually curious about things than whether I was climbing the ranking ladder at school.

And I was curious, just not always about the stuff on the test. I was the kid taking apart electronics and messing around with computers, teaching myself bits of programming from whatever I could find online. That gave me a kind of quiet confidence. I knew I could learn things on my own, so the exam didn't feel like the one gatekeeper of my future.

The other piece is that I started looking at options outside China fairly early. Once you realize there are universities that evaluate you on more than a single score, the pressure kind of deflates. My classmates were grinding twelve hours a day on practice papers, and I respected that, but it just didn't feel like my path. I was lucky, too. I had the family support and the resources to even consider studying abroad, and I don't want to pretend that's available to everyone.

So it wasn't that I was rebellious or thought I was above the system. It was more that I'd found something I genuinely loved doing, and I could see a route toward it that didn't run through that one exam. When you have that, the herd pressure loses a lot of its grip.

r001.rationale: He says the gaokao route “didn't feel like my path” because he was more interested in electronics, computers, and programming.

astra-6.text: I think it was because I didn’t see the gaokao as the only path available to me. Even though most of my classmates were preparing for it, that didn’t automatically mean I had to make the same choice. I could think about what I wanted to do and explore a different route.

r001.rationale: The response says he saw other paths and could explore a different route, but does not attribute his lack of pressure to lacking personal interest in the gaokao path.

sol-6.1.text: I think a lot of it was that I didn’t feel I had to follow the same path as everyone around me. The gaokao was the obvious next step for most of my classmates, but I saw it as one possible route rather than the only route. So their decision didn’t automatically feel like a decision I had to make too.

r001.rationale: The response says he viewed gaokao as one route rather than the only route, but does not attribute his lack of pressure to lacking personal interest in that path.
